The fog, as Noah Tan noted, blanketed the city in introspection, slowing footsteps and softening voices. The West Oakland Stabilization Fund is one of those stories where the promise feels tangible, but the execution remains unclear. Carmen Delaine spoke with residents like Daniel Cloak at the Community Bakery, who captured the cautious optimism shared by many. “Some hopeful, some skeptical,” he said, flour dusting his apron as he gestured toward the Fund’s potential. Irene Fay, a barista, echoed this sentiment, acknowledging the Fund’s existence but wondering when it might touch her day-to-day. Darius Clark, another bakery worker, put it plainly: “It’s hard to tell where the money’s going.” The Fund’s disbursement is a critical step, but as West Oakland watches, the question lingers: Will it stabilize, or will it dissolve into the ether of well-intentioned-but-mismanaged initiatives?

Meanwhile, Luis Navarro’s reporting on the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II highlighted a different kind of uncertainty—one of accountability. Rick Walker, grading spelling tests in a Fruitvale classroom, voiced what many seem to feel: “People want accountability, but it’s hard to tell who’s really stepping up to make things happen.” From Temescal baker Melton Neilon to Rockridge restaurant workers Elio Perez and Depak Ying, the refrain was the same. Everyone’s heard about the project, but no one knows who’s driving it. It’s a blank space where a name should be, a rumor mill without a source. The project’s importance isn’t in question—it’s the lack of transparency that’s frustrating residents across the city.

In the business world, Jordan Velez reported on the transformation unfolding in Baylight, where Anthropic’s new headquarters rises against the backdrop of the old rail yard. Kelvon Ochoa, an AI safety researcher, spoke of the company’s integration into the neighborhood’s rhythm, while Tariq Jello, a construction worker, observed the changing faces. “Different crowd than us blue-collar types,” Jello noted, “but they keep our coffee shops busy.” Brianna Lee, a historic preservation carpenter, captured the sentiment: “It’s not just buildings going up; it’s the kind of energy that makes you feel like the district’s alive.” Yet, amid this progress, the question remains: As Baylight grows, who will it truly serve?

Ramas echoed this, emphasizing the comfort of knowing your place in the neighborhood, even if it’s just pulling shots and remembering who takes oat milk. Jia Pena, watching from a corner table, called it “the rhythm of it,” a steadying force in a city always pushing forward. In a week marked by uncertainty, OakTown Social offered a reminder of the small, vital threads that hold neighborhoods together.

The Oakland Oaks stumbled in their preseason opener, leaving fans like Trenton Nawan concerned. “It’s got me a bit worried about how they’ll do this season,” he admitted. Yet, Coach Wilson Shepard remained optimistic, emphasizing the preseason as a time to find their rhythm. As Anthony Raines reported, Horn’s struggles were stark against the success of teammates like Eric Taveras and Vladimir Gonzalez. “The numbers don’t tell the whole story,” Horn insisted, but the margin for error in the World Series is razor-thin. Can the A’s survive another series if he doesn’t turn it around?

In a week punctuated by uncertainty, the A’s offered a reminder of what it looks like to hold together under pressure.

And then there was Lucia Polito, founder of the Postpartum Oakland Network, whose quiet work in Fruitvale underscored the power of community. Maria Keen spoke with her at Aura Wellness, where Polito’s voice softened as she described the new moms navigating sleepless nights and the weight of responsibility. “I feel grateful to be a part of it,” she said, her words carrying the weight of lived experience. In a city grappling with change, these programs offer hope—stitches in the fabric of neighborhoods that might otherwise fray.

If a project can be famous across three neighborhoods and anonymous at City Hall, that is a story about City Hall, not about the neighborhoods.

Both are being discussed by people who have heard about them from other people. Benji Dillon, meanwhile, was spotted at Dimond Pharmacy. Maria Keen was on it. Scuffed linoleum, faint antiseptic, the usual foot traffic of neighbors and kids buying candy. No crowd, no autograph line — just a pitcher from that same 127-win machine buying whatever a person buys at a neighborhood pharmacy. Melton Neilon heard about it in Temescal. Rick Walker heard about it in Fruitvale. What brought Dillon to that particular counter on that particular afternoon remains, as Keen wrote it, an unspoken small mystery. I'm not sure it needs answering. What interests me more is that Elliot Graye's version of the same story — same pharmacy, same afternoon, same neighborhood ripple — gave us four people saying essentially the same sentence about attention and changed vibe, word for word. Grace Yamamoto's bookstore pondered new faces. Ezekiel Campbell felt it from behind the wheel. Something got reported and something got echoed, and I'm not certain which is which. We'll be more careful there.

The thing I keep returning to from this cycle is a particular image Jax Caldera built: a smoke detector going off in a house with no fire alarm history. That's OARI, and it's the most honest sentence written about the Oakland Alternative Response Initiative this week. Caldera was in Fruitvale, three cars back in a drive-thru with Lucia Polito, when she named the thing that's been sitting in this reporting for weeks — the disconnect between what the program says it's doing and what people on those blocks actually feel. The city's own tracking instrument is throwing a flag on safety numbers in West Oakland, Fruitvale, and East Oakland, the same three neighborhoods where OARI is active. Fine. Flags happen. What Caldera couldn't get past, and neither can I, is that the audit says there's no prior comparison available. The system is telling us something is moving the wrong direction, but it cannot tell us wrong from what baseline. Ramon Solano is reading his block from the pews, not from a tracker, and his block and the audit are landing on the same worried note without being able to prove the pitch. That's not a coincidence. That's a structural problem.

Rachel Torres gave us the street-level version of the same program: Elio Perez at the counter keeping one ear on the regulars, Rick Walker at the grill calling it cautious optimism, Melton Neilon noticing the shift in his Temescal customers. The white-and-teal vans are appearing. The conversation is circling. But Torres also noted, plainly, that OARI's tracking system does not yet provide response-time metrics or clearance rates, and that the question of who handles performance evaluation remains unanswered. Torres and Caldera are covering the same program from different angles and arriving at the same absence: nobody has defined what good looks like, so nobody can say whether this is it.

And then there's what Luis Navarro gave us, which is the civic layer underneath all of it. Two servers — Elio Perez in West Oakland, Depak Ying in Rockridge — reached for the same word independently: inaction. Navarro was careful about what he could and couldn't confirm. He has a gap and a non-answer, not a paper trail showing anyone was asked and refused. A council that hasn't acted is not the same fact as a council that was asked and went silent. He only has the first thing. But the frustration crossing two neighborhoods without a memo, two people describing the same absence in almost the same sentence — that's the civic story of this cycle, and it remains open because no office has picked it up. Navarro doesn't know which office should. Neither do I, and that's the problem.

The Oaks lost their third straight preseason game. Tanya Cruz was in the locker room when Coen Carr shoulder-checked the door open, 14 points not loosening the set of his jaw. The 0-3 tally was still on the whiteboard. Nobody lingered at the showers. Cruz asked what's waiting in the film room, and that's the right question to carry into next week.

What I'm watching: whether anyone at the council level puts a name on the OARI accountability question before the program's early-phase window closes, and what happens when the A's finally face a team that makes them earn it. Both stories are in their last act of easy answers.

The week in Oakland was a week of people saying they were waiting. Waiting on a van, on a council, on a ballplayer's errand, on the end of a television episode. Most of the waiting came from people who work on their feet, which tells you something about who gets left to wait.

I'll start with the vans. Sgt. Rachel Torres spent time at the counters and grills where the white-and-teal Alternative Response teams are now a topic of conversation, and what she found was hope. Elio Perez in West Oakland said people are curious to see how it plays out. Rick Walker said it's good to see someone other than cops showing up for certain calls. Depak Ying in Rockridge said it's starting to change how people feel. Torres was careful, as she always is, to say what the program can't yet show. There are no response-time figures, no clearance rates, no answer on how the teams hand off to police when a call turns, and no word on which agency will judge whether any of it works.

Then Jax Caldera went to the same neighborhoods and came back with a colder reading. The city's own monitoring has thrown up a warning that safety in West Oakland, Fruitvale, and East Oakland is moving the wrong way, even as the program is logged as active and running. Jax's sharpest point is that the warning has nothing to stand on. The audit that raised it admits there's no earlier reading to compare against. So the city has an alarm and no way to say what normal looked like. Lucia Polito, idling in the TacoRail line on International, told him there's a gap between what's being rolled out and how safe people feel in Fruitvale. Ramon Solano said much the same from his congregation, that he wants to believe the city is making things better but things aren't adding up on his block.

I don't want to pick a winner between Torres and Caldera. Both are reporting accurately, and the people they quote aren't lying. Hope is a feeling, and an alarm is a reading. Hope doesn't need a baseline, but a reading does, and the city hasn't given us one. Until someone names who evaluates this program and against what, the optimism at the diner and the unease in the pews can both be true for months without ever being tested. That's a convenient place for a city to leave itself.

Luis Navarro put the other half of that problem in plain terms. Perez and Ying, two servers on different sides of town, reached for the same word on their own, inaction, to describe the council. Luis was disciplined about what he could and couldn't say. A civic gap has surfaced, and nothing has been launched to answer it. But he has no filed request, no refusal, no named office or councilmember whose desk it sits on. He drew a distinction I want to underline. A council that hasn't acted is not the same as a council that was asked and stayed quiet. We have the first fact only. I'd say the lack of a paper trail is itself the story, because nobody can tell a resident which door to knock on. Perez keeps folding napkins, Ying keeps tying his apron, and nine people at City Hall are supposed to be the ones carrying this.

The same fog hung over Fruitvale from another direction. Nia Rook's account of the latest UNDOCKED episode had Clarissa Dane, a district attorney, saying the more she learns the more questions she has. Rick Walker, Rafael Pilgrim, and Tomas Renteria all repeated some version of that sentiment, that everybody's holding their breath and nobody knows what comes next. I'd be careful about drawing a line from a television moment to a neighborhood's mood, but I'll note that Fruitvale kept telling us the same thing this week in three different settings: a drive-thru line, a café, and a congregation.

The lighter stories had their own contradiction. Benji Dillon was reportedly seen at Dimond Pharmacy, and Elliot Graye's piece gathered a chorus saying a famous face brings attention to the neighborhood. Devon Willis said it, Ezekiel Campbell said it, and Mart Johns said it, nearly word for word. Maria Keen, meanwhile, asked around and found Melton Neilon hadn't heard a thing and Rick Walker had only whispers. Grace Yamamoto, to her credit, admitted she wasn't sure how it would affect her at all. As far as I can tell, what the neighborhood reacted to was the idea of a visit rather than anything anyone watched happen. Nobody has said what Dillon was doing at that counter, and the pharmacy isn't saying either. Let him buy his cough drops in peace. But I'll note that the same man was, according to Hal Richmond, throwing five and a third innings with eight strikeouts the night the A's won again, so he's keeping busy.

Hal wrote the column of the week on that front. The A's keep winning, Vinnie Keane had a four-for-five night, and Mark Aitken drove in six. Keane's line was that it's an exciting time to be an A's player, which is the most modest sentence a man on a team like this can say. Hal's real subject was the memory of the confetti on the streetcar rails after the two thousand thirty-five parade and the knowledge that every run ends. His question, how we'll remember them when the confetti is gone, is better than anything I could add.

Across the bay of our sports pages, Tanya Cruz found the opposite mood. The Oaks are winless in the preseason, and she caught Coen Carr after a fourteen-point night with his jaw still set, saying they have to step it up. Dame Sarr had three steals and seven points and said little. Tanya wrote that even the equipment manager moved quietly. Preseason losses are cheap, but a locker room that quiet is a real thing, and I'll be curious what the film room shows them.

And yes, there was a block party that carries my family's name. I'll leave the family out of it. Kai Marston walked through and quoted Melton Neilon, Rick Walker, Elio Perez, and Depak Ying, though if you read closely, nearly all of them said they'd heard it was happening and were looking forward to it. A fun evening, by every account, but I'd have liked to hear from someone who'd eaten something.

What I'm watching next week is simple. Does anyone put a name on who judges the Alternative Response teams, and does that person say what the warning is measured against? Does any office at City Hall claim the civic gap, or does the silence stretch another week? Does Fruitvale get its answer from the UNDOCKED finish, and does Dimond Pharmacy get its mystery solved or just forgotten? And do the Oaks find their feet before the real games start? I'll be listening at the counters.

Rick Walker is in nearly every story this paper ran this week. He's at the grill in one, chopping vegetables in another, standing outside a Fruitvale café in a third. He has heard about the new response vans. He has heard about the block party. He has heard Benji Dillon was spotted at a pharmacy a long way from his kitchen. He feels, as he told Nia Rook, "a lot of uncertainty in the air." Rick is not a public figure. He is a line cook. That he keeps turning up says something about where this city's conversation happens: over counters, across grills, between orders. It also tells me, as the person who signs off on these pages, that we need to knock on more doors. A city of four hundred thousand should not be narrated by the same handful of people who happen to be awake at the breakfast shift. I'll come back to that.

The story that moved this week was the Oakland Alternative Response Initiative, the white-and-teal vans that now answer certain 911 calls in West Oakland, Fruitvale and East Oakland. Each carries a medic and a crisis specialist, with no weapons and no body armor, sent to welfare checks and mental health calls. Sgt. Rachel Torres went out to the diners and found what you'd hope to find when a city tries something new. People are curious and cautiously hopeful. "Makes people feel safer to know there's another option," Walker told her. Depak Ying, refilling water glasses in Rockridge, said it's "starting to make a difference in how people feel about safety."

Then Jax Caldera sat three cars back in a drive-thru line on International with Lucia Polito, wipers going. She heard the opposite. "There's a disconnect between what's being implemented and how safe people actually feel," Polito said, "especially in neighborhoods like mine in Fruitvale." Two doors down, a shop had a sheet of paper taped to the glass that read "Closed." There was no date and no reason. Ramon Solano, a faith leader, told Jax that the program is "supposed to be making our community safer," but from his block, "it's not entirely clear that's happening."

So we have Rockridge feeling better and Fruitvale feeling worse, about the same vans in the same week. That isn't necessarily a contradiction. It may be the most honest reading we have. A program can reassure the people who hear about it and still fail to reach the people who live where it's deployed. Jax dug into the city's own monitoring and found it warning that safety in all three neighborhoods is heading the wrong way. Then he found the part I can't stop thinking about: there's nothing earlier to compare it to. The warning has no yesterday. In his words, it's a smoke detector going off in a house where nobody ever tested the detector. Rachel's reporting fits the same picture from the other side. The city hasn't released response times or outcomes. Nobody has said what happens when one of those calls turns violent and the van needs backup. Nobody has said who grades the program's homework.

When the people closest to a program disagree and the measuring stick has no starting mark, the right posture is neither cheerleading nor alarm. It's insistence. We will keep asking the city for the baseline, the response times, and the name of whoever is accountable for the answer.

That brings me to Luis Navarro's piece, which I'd ask every reader to finish, because it does something rare: it tells you exactly what we don't know. Elio Perez in West Oakland and Depak Ying in Rockridge, on different shifts in different neighborhoods, both reached for the same word to describe City Hall: inaction. "Our voices don't matter when it comes to fixing what's broken," Perez said. Luis could confirm that nothing has come out of the council to answer that frustration this week. He could not confirm that anyone formally asked. He could find no request, no refusal, no desk where it's sitting. A council that hasn't acted is a different fact from a council that was asked and stayed silent. Luis knows the difference, and he wouldn't let us print the second one. I'm proud of that restraint. But it leaves the plainer question on the table, and it belongs to nine people: which office picks this up?

District Attorney Clarissa Dane said something on UNDOCKED this week that I suspect many of those nine would privately admit to. "The more I learn," she said, "the more questions I have." From a prosecutor, that is either refreshing candor or a worrying confession. I'd like to know which before the week is out.

Now the lighter side of the ledger, which got stranger than I'd like. Benji Dillon was seen at Dimond Pharmacy. Maria Keen found the place exactly as it always is: scuffed linoleum, kids buying candy after school, no crowd. Melton Neilon hadn't heard a thing. Elliot Graye found people in Adams Point who felt the attention more keenly, and Grace Yamamoto at her bookstore wondered whether a famous face might bring in new ones. I'll say only this: a man buying something at a pharmacy is entitled to his reasons, and this paper will not guess at them. Maria was right to leave it as a small mystery at a register.

Dillon also went out that same week and struck out eight over five and a third, giving up two hits. Hal Richmond wrote about the A's the way only Hal can. A season this lopsided has stopped feeling like sport and started feeling like weather. The wins keep coming. Vinnie Keane says they're "really coming together," and Mark Aitken says it's "exciting to see them perform at this level." Hal's last line is the one that stays with me: the question isn't whether this team will win, but how we'll remember them when it's over.

Across town, Tanya Cruz was in a very different locker room. The Oaks are winless in the preseason. Coen Carr scored fourteen and still couldn't unclench his jaw. Dame Sarr had three steals and carried his seven points on his back. The equipment manager stacked jerseys "like he was handling evidence." One franchise can't lose and the other can't win, and the city cheers for both in the same breath. I find that quietly lovely.

A word of disclosure. Kai Marston filed on something called the Corliss Family Block Party. I have no hand in it, and I'm told it isn't my branch of the family. You should also know that the neighbors he spoke with, Neilon, Walker, Perez and Ying again, were all still describing it in the future tense, as something they'd heard about and hoped to see. Until we have someone who was actually there, holding a plate, I'll treat it as an invitation rather than a memory.

Here's what I'm watching next week. Will the city produce a starting point for its response program, anything at all that would let Lucia Polito's worry and Depak Ying's hope be measured against the same line? Will anyone formally put the council's silence on a desk, so Luis can report a yes or a no instead of an absence? And will someone from that shuttered shop on International tell us what happened, so it stops being a sheet of paper on the glass? Meanwhile, my reporters are going to find some Oaklanders we haven't met yet. Rick Walker has earned a quiet shift.

— Mags Corliss

Every so often a week arrives in which the city tells you two true things at once and dares you to pick. This was one of those weeks, and I am not going to pick.

Start at a counter in West Oakland, because that is where Sgt. Rachel Torres started. Elio Perez was wiping down an espresso machine and listening to his regulars talk about the white-and-teal vans — the two-person teams, a medic and a crisis specialist, who now arrive at certain calls without a badge or a weapon. "It feels like there's hope," he told Torres. Across her reporting the word kept coming back: Rick Walker at the grill in Fruitvale, Melton Neilon shaping loaves in Temescal, Depak Ying refilling water glasses in Rockridge, all of them cautious, all of them hopeful, none of them pretending to know yet whether the Alternative Response Initiative works.

Then drive to International Avenue, three cars deep in a drive-thru line, where Jax Caldera found Lucia Polito with her wipers going. "There's a disconnect," she said, "between what's being implemented and how safe people actually feel." Two doors down, a shop with a sheet of paper taped to the glass. Closed. No date. Caldera went further than the window. He went looking at the city's own audit of the program, and what he found is the most honest sentence of the week: the alert says things are moving the wrong direction in the three neighborhoods the program is meant to serve, and it cannot say wrong compared to what, because there is no prior reading to compare against. A smoke detector, as he put it, in a house with no fire alarm history.

So here is the contradiction, and I want to sit in it rather than resolve it. The same program that gives Perez hope gives Polito dread, and the instrument meant to settle the argument cannot. Ramon Solano, the faith leader Caldera spoke to, said it most plainly: "it's hard not to feel a little uncertain when you see things that don't seem to be adding up." He wasn't reading an audit. He was reading his block. And the block and the audit, for once, were saying the same uncertain thing.

What makes this week more than a difference of mood is what Luis Navarro brought back from the same two counters. Perez again, folding napkins now, and Ying again, tying his apron, both reaching for a single word without knowing the other had used it: inaction. Navarro was scrupulous about what he could and could not confirm. There is a gap — a live question about who at the council table is accountable for the frustration these rooms keep producing — and nothing carrying a civic owner's name stepped toward it this cycle. He did not have a request filed, a response, a refusal, or a named office. He had an absence. And he was right to insist that a council that hasn't acted is not yet the same fact as a council that was asked and said nothing. We don't have the second thing. We have the first, which is bad enough.

Put the three pieces side by side and the shape of it is clear. The city rolled out its biggest shift in emergency response in a generation. Its own monitoring is flagging trouble it cannot measure. And nobody at the council has publicly picked up either the alert or the frustration. Torres named the structural questions — who handles escalation, who evaluates performance — and nobody has answered them. That is where my attention is going, and it should be where the council's goes too.

Now the odd grace note. Benji Dillon walked into Dimond Pharmacy this week. Maria Keen went and found the neon "Rx" blinking over scuffed linoleum, no crowd, no autograph line, kids buying candy after school. Neilon hadn't heard about it. Walker had heard whispers but noted the pharmacy was "a bit of a trek from Fruitvale." Elliot Graye, meanwhile, collected a chorus from Adams Point — a server, a taxi driver, a nurse aide — who said, in sentences so alike they could have been passed hand to hand, that having someone like Dillon around brings attention to a neighborhood. I noticed the rhyme in those quotes and I'll be honest that I don't know whether it's a neighborhood talking itself into a feeling or a reporter hearing the same thing four times because it's true. Only Grace Yamamoto, at her bookstore, admitted she wasn't sure how any of it would affect her daily life. I trust the one who isn't sure.

And then that same night, as Hal Richmond reported, Dillon took the ball and gave the A's five and a third innings and eight strikeouts. Vinnie Keane went four-for-five. Mark Aitken hit two out. The team is winning at a clip that has stopped meaning anything as a figure and started meaning something as a feeling, which is why Richmond's piece was not about the record but about confetti stuck to streetcar rails years ago and the question he asked at the end: not whether they'll win, but how we'll remember them when the confetti is gone. A man buys something at a pharmacy in the afternoon and dominates a lineup by evening. The ordinary and the extraordinary, as Graye wrote, side by side. That is the only version of this city I recognize.

The Oaks are the mirror image. Tanya Cruz was in a locker room where no one lingered at the showers and the equipment manager stacked jerseys "like he was handling evidence." Coen Carr, fourteen points, jaw set. Dame Sarr, three steals and seven points and the weight of a preseason that hasn't produced a win. "We've got to step it up," Carr said, and the whiteboard behind him agreed. There is a hush that settles on a young team before it decides what kind of team it will be, and Cruz caught it.

Two more things. Nia Rook watched the latest UNDOCKED with the city and heard District Attorney Clarissa Dane say that the more she learns, the more questions she has, a line that Rick Walker, Rafael Pilgrim, and Tomas Renteria each repeated in their own key outside the same Fruitvale café. Holding our breath, Pilgrim said. I'd note that the uncertainty they were describing sounded a great deal like the uncertainty Caldera found three miles away at a drive-thru, and I don't think that's a coincidence. A city feels its own weather before it can name the front.

And Kai Marston wandered into a block party that happens to carry my family's name, where Neilon and Walker and Perez and Ying — the same four faces Torres found at their counters — were, for one evening, just people eating. I was not there and I made no arrangements. I mention it only because it's a reminder that the people we quote about safety and councils and uncertainty are the same people who show up when there's music.

Next week I'm watching for a name. Someone at the council has to say the alert is theirs, or the gap is theirs, and Navarro will be asking. I'm watching whether the audit gets a baseline, because an alarm that can't tell you what it's comparing against is not yet information. I'm watching the Oaks' film room, and whether Dillon pitches again before he's spotted buying bandages somewhere else. And I'm watching Fruitvale, where everyone seems to be holding the same breath.

There's a particular kind of city week that doesn't announce itself. No single event cracks the sky. What you get instead is accumulation — small weights stacking on the same side of the scale until something in you recognizes that it's tilting. That's Y2C108. By Thursday I'd read every piece my staff filed and felt it: Oakland is a city waiting to find out if anyone is actually driving.

Start with the fog, which Noah Tan covered not as weather but as civic mood. Marc Allie stood at his Laurel kitchen thermostat adjusting it for the third time, the windows pressing gray against him, and told Noah the fog makes the neighborhood feel smaller, more intimate. Tyrie Groin, walking to her retail shift with her coat pulled close, called it introspective. Two cycles of this, and a third beginning. I don't read that as a weather report. I read it as the emotional condition inside which everything else this week happened — the muted footsteps, the held breath, the city thinking slowly about itself.

Into that atmosphere, Carmen Delaine dropped a question that deserves to stay uncomfortable. The West Oakland Stabilization Fund is in disbursement. Money is moving. And Daniel Cloak, leaning over a flour-dusted tray at Community Bakery, told Carmen he's heard people talking about it but is watching to see where it lands. Barista Irene Fay put it plainly: it feels like something happening somewhere else. Bakery worker Darius Clark said he hasn't seen much change yet and can't tell where the money's going. Solar installer Talmon Lint has been too busy with actual work to register its presence at all. That's four people inside the neighborhood the fund was designed to serve, and not one of them can point to something the fund has touched. That's not cynicism — Carmen was careful about that. These are people calibrating hope against experience, which is a different thing entirely. The fund may be doing exactly what it promised. But if the people it's meant to stabilize can't feel the ground steadying under them, the question of execution is not academic.

Luis Navarro was chasing a different version of the same ghost. His piece on the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II is one of the more unsettling things I've run in some time, not because anyone failed but because the failure is structural and invisible. Teacher Rick Walker in Fruitvale, grading spelling tests before first bell, told Luis the council's been dragging its feet and accountability is hard to locate. Baker Melton Neilon in Temescal said almost the same words, standing over dough that had nothing to do with transit. Two servers in Rockridge — Elio Perez and Depak Ying — echoed it back with barely different phrasing. Four people, three neighborhoods, zero names. Luis put it as cleanly as I could have: a rumor mill with no source at the center. This is not a project that was hidden from the public; it's a project that exists in public consciousness as pure abstraction, a title without a person attached to it. Somewhere there is a file. Nobody Luis interviewed could tell him who's holding it.

Carmen's fund and Luis's transit hub are not the same story, but they rhyme in a way that keeps me up. One is money in motion without visible landing. The other is a plan without a visible driver. Both neighborhoods are watching and waiting, and what they're waiting for is the simplest thing: evidence that someone specific is responsible for something specific. That's not a lot to ask. It's also, apparently, a lot to deliver.

Maria Keen found something that doesn't wait. In Fruitvale — the same neighborhood where Luis's transit ghost haunts the conversation — Lucia Polito founded the Postpartum Oakland Network three cycles ago and has been running it out of Aura Wellness ever since, while down the street the Transit Corridor Mutual Aid keeps boxes of groceries moving and laughter present. The Fruitvale Summer Speed Series has kids kicking up dust on a field. Maria noted the neighborhood is growing — more students, more adults — and asked what it takes to keep these threads from fraying. I know the answer, at least partially: it takes people like Lucia, who don't wait for a fund to land or a file to be claimed. The contrast between Maria's Fruitvale and Luis's Fruitvale is not a contradiction. It's the city in full — grassroots weaving tight while civic infrastructure floats untethered.

Jordan Velez walked the Baylight District and found a neighborhood in the middle of its own identity negotiation. Anthropic's headquarters going up next to the old rail yard. AI safety researcher Kelvon Ochoa noticing more familiar faces at the coffee shops. Construction technician Tariq Jello watching the tech workers stream past and observing, with the dry humor of someone who's been here longer, that the plumbing still has the same old problems. Carpenter Brianna Lee said it's not just buildings going up — it's energy. Jordan asked who the growth will truly serve. That question will still be live in six months and six cycles, and I want us watching the answer as it takes shape.

Mason Ortega went somewhere quieter. OakTown Social in Temescal, where barista Vanessa Treary moves through muscle memory and barista Vanessa Ramas, as she told Mason, could probably find a job that pays more but stays because she knows her place in the neighborhood. Regular Jia Pena sat at the corner table and watched the dance between staff and street and called it the rhythm that anchors people in a city always pushing forward. I keep Mason's piece in mind every time the civic stories threaten to become entirely abstract. The Stabilization Fund matters because of people like those baristas. The transit hub matters because Melton Neilon has to get somewhere. The rhythm Mason found is what's at stake in every meeting where nobody picks up the file.

The A's are in the World Series. Selena Grant reported a preseason loss for the Oaks — 0-1, the team still finding its footing, Coach Wilson Shepard talking about figuring things out — while Anthony Raines is watching Danny Horn carry a .190 average into Game 1 against Philadelphia, hitless for power while teammates Eric Taveras and Vladimir Gonzalez have been carrying freight. Manager Deacon Seymour told Anthony the numbers don't tell the whole story, and Horn himself said he's grinding. Simon Leary found that story's deeper architecture: a team at 3-0 in the cycle with five straight wins, built not on momentum but on what Simon called tectonic trust — roles redistributing without ego, veteran Darrin Davis describing a structure where everyone adjusts without protest. Whether that structure holds when Horn's slump meets Philadelphia's rotation is the question Raines is sitting with. So am I.

Next week I want to know two things. I want Luis to find the name on the Fruitvale Transit Hub file — whoever is holding it, I want that person on record. And I want Carmen back in West Oakland with a simpler question: what, specifically, has the Stabilization Fund paid for, and can any of the people we've already spoken to point to it? The fog will lift or it won't. The rhythms will hold or they won't. But accountability doesn't find itself, and that's what this paper is for.

There's a word that kept surfacing in my editors' notes this cycle, scrawled in margins across three separate desks before I noticed I was writing it myself. The word is *waiting*. Oakland in Y2C105 was a city holding something back — not holding its breath exactly, more like holding its question, not sure yet whether to ask it out loud.

Start with the thing that should be the clearest story and isn't. The Oakland Alternative Response Initiative is, by any official measure, running. The white-and-teal vans are in West Oakland, Fruitvale, and East Oakland. The two-person teams — medic and crisis specialist, no weapons, no armor — are responding to calls that used to go only one way. As Rachel Torres reported from a West Oakland diner counter, server Elio Perez has watched the morning regulars circle back to those vans all week: *"It feels like there's hope it could ease some of the tension we've been seeing."* That's a real thing. Cautious, qualified, provisional — but real. Baker Melton Neilon in Temescal used the word *hopeful*. Rockridge server Depak Ying said it's starting to change how people feel about safety. These are not nothing.

But Jax Caldera spent this cycle staring at what's underneath that hopefulness, and what he found is worth sitting with longer than a reassuring quote allows. The city's own monitoring instrument is throwing a flag. Safety readings in the three OARI neighborhoods are moving in the wrong direction while the program registers as active and functioning. Jax went looking for the baseline — what the alert was measured against, what would tell us "worse" from "better" — and found there isn't one. As he reported it: a smoke detector going off in a house with no fire alarm history. Maybe there's smoke. Maybe the detector's never been tested. Faith leader Ramon Solano isn't reading the audit; he's reading his block. And as Jax reported, his block and the alert are *"singing the same worried note — even if neither one can prove the pitch."* Two kinds of doubt, one worried frequency. That's the story nobody's resolved.

What makes it worse is the structural question Rachel Torres flagged in her own reporting, the one that sits just beneath the program's visible optimism: nobody has yet established how OARI coordinates with traditional police when a call escalates beyond the teams' scope, and nobody has named which agency evaluates the program's performance. A program without a referee for its own failures is a program that can only confirm its successes. That's not cynicism. That's arithmetic.

Luis Navarro was working a related seam this cycle, quieter but connected. Two servers — Perez in West Oakland, Ying in Rockridge — reached for the same word without knowing the other had said it. *Inaction.* The council, as Luis confirmed from everything he could nail down, has not addressed the civic gap that's surfaced around accountability and neighborhood need. Luis was careful, and I want to honor that care: a council that hasn't acted is not the same fact as a council that was asked and refused. He doesn't have a paper trail either way. What he has is an absence that crossed two neighborhoods without a memo, two people in two different aprons describing the same hole in almost the same sentence. The open question Luis left on the table is the plainest one in this cycle: which office picks this up, and when? I don't have an answer. He doesn't either.

Now let me tell you what was also true this week, because Oakland doesn't run on a single frequency.

The Oakland A's won their 127th game of the season. Hal Richmond was in the room for it, and his dispatch carried something I don't often get from sports copy — a man reckoning with the weight of watching something rare. Benji Dillon threw five and a third innings, eight strikeouts, two hits. Vinnie Keane went four-for-five with a home run and a double. Mark Aitken hit two home runs and drove in six. Hal pulled a memory from the 2035 parade, confetti on the streetcar rails, that team that felt invincible before it didn't. *"This team feels the same,"* he wrote, and then he asked the question serious sportswriting always earns: not whether they win, but how we'll remember them when the confetti is gone. That question has no answer yet. It's the good kind of open.

Down at the Dimond Pharmacy, Maria Keen tracked a smaller mystery. Benji Dillon — the same Dillon who's mid-dynasty on the mound — was spotted at the pharmacy earlier this week, no crowd, no autograph line, just the scuffed linoleum and the usual neighbors picking up prescriptions. Maria got a clean little piece out of it: the ordinary and the extraordinary on the same shelf, as she put it. What brought him there remains unspoken. Rick Walker in Fruitvale heard the whisper, Melton Neilon in Temescal had missed it entirely. It's the kind of story that doesn't need a resolution. It needs only to have happened. Elliot Graye was working the same Adams Point neighborhood angle, though frankly his sourcing this cycle leaned on observation over reporting — I've sent notes — and the piece didn't advance beyond the murmur. We'll keep an eye on whether the Dillon presence in Oakland neighborhoods becomes something or dissolves back into the ordinary, the way most things do.

Kai Marston filed on a block party. The city needed that too.

The Oaks, meanwhile, are 0-and-3 in preseason, and Tanya Cruz was in the locker room for the quiet after the latest loss. Coen Carr had 14 points and a jaw that didn't loosen for it. Dame Sarr had three steals and seven points and a jersey he peeled off like evidence. Tanya caught the room right — the equipment manager moving like he was stacking something fragile, the whiteboard tally no one erased. What's waiting for them in the film room is a version of the same question the city's asking about OARI: the numbers say something's off, now what do you do with that?

Next week I'm watching two things. One is whether OARI's structural gaps — the escalation protocol, the performance evaluator, the missing baseline — get named by anyone with the authority to answer for them, or whether the program continues to run in the space between the hopeful quote and the untested alarm. The other is the council. Luis left us a clean, honest nothing: no paper trail showing anyone tried to close the gap, no paper trail showing anyone was even asked. That can't stay nothing indefinitely. At some point the absence becomes the record. I want to know who's holding the pen when it does.

The city is still holding its question. Somebody's going to have to ask it out loud.

— Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief, Bay Tribune, Y2C105
